The [starter](../../starters/mps2-an385-bare-metal.md) scaffolded a Rust
talker for `board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"`, ran it in QEMU over the board's
serial port, and heard it from ROS 2. This page covers what comes after it:
moving the image onto the board's network, what is particular to a board with
no operating system, the run plan, and driving cargo yourself.

Use bare-metal for very constrained Cortex-M targets with no scheduler and no
threads. If your target has FreeRTOS or another RTOS, the
[FreeRTOS on mps2-an385](freertos.md) page is the same board with a
scheduler under your nodes.

## Configure the platform

The whole deployment is the bringup's `system.toml`, compiled into the image:
the generated entry folds the image's network identity into the
configuration the board applies at boot. There is no configuration file on
the device and no `.cargo/` to edit. The target triple, linker script,
`--gc-sections` flag, QEMU runner and the `[patch.crates-io]` rows that
resolve nano-ros's crates all come from the board, and `nros build` writes
them under `build/`.

The starter's image reaches the router over the board's serial port, the
first link a real board's program uses. To reach it over the board's
ethernet instead, on QEMU's user-mode network, give the image a TCP
`locator` and an address:

```toml
[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:10500"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]
```

and the address, in a board network file beside `system.toml` in the
bringup:

```toml
[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10
```

The board package owns the network device, so the device's address lives in
the board's own file, which the image names with `os_config`. `10.0.2.2` is
QEMU's gateway to the host. With this `locator`, `nros run bm_node` starts
the router on the host's port 10500 when it boots the image. If a zenoh
router of your own already listens on that port, `nros run` uses it instead
and says so; anything else on the port stops the run before it starts, naming
`--router`. Within
about 15 seconds of boot the zenoh session opens and the first
`Publishing:` line appears.

Changing `board` to `"mps2-an385-freertos"` and building again builds the
FreeRTOS image of the same node, with no other edit: the node package's
`Cargo.toml` names no board crate, RMW backend or panic handler. Those are the
generated entry's dependencies.

## Board notes

- **QEMU's MPS2-AN385, a Cortex-M3.** The board crate is
  `nros-board-mps2-an385`, with no `-freertos` suffix: it carries the
  Cortex-M3 startup, the linker script, the LAN9118 ethernet driver for
  smoltcp and the idle wait (`wfi`).
- **One entry shape: direct execution.** The generated entry runs your
  executor in one loop on the reset path. `qemu-arm-baremetal` is a retired
  spelling of the same board; use `mps2-an385-baremetal`.
- **Rust only.** The C and C++ APIs assume an RTOS's startup, heap and libc,
  so they do not build here.
- **No `alloc` by default.** The build is `no_std` with `heapless`
  collections. To use `alloc`, enable the board crate's `alloc` feature and
  supply a `#[global_allocator]`.
- **No preemption and no wake primitive.** Callbacks run one at a time in the
  loop. A callback that runs long holds back every other callback until it
  returns.
- **The console is semihosting,** so QEMU prints the image's output on your
  terminal.
- **Nothing is flashed.** `mps2-an385` is a QEMU machine, and `nros setup`
  provisions no probe or flash tooling for it. A real Cortex-M board is a
  board package of your own; [Add a board](../../extending/add-a-board.md#example)
  takes an STM32F4-Discovery through it, and
  [Flash a real board](flash-a-real-board.md) flashes the result.

## Read the run plan

From the starter's workspace, print the plan `nros run` follows:

```bash probe=410
nros run bm_node --dry-run --why
```

The parts that matter, trimmed, for the starter's serial image:

```text
[runner]
package = "nros_runner_qemu"
name = "qemu"

[target]
emulator = "qemu:mps2-an385"

[console]
kind = "semihosting"

[link]
kind = "serial"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"
rmw = "zenoh"
host_peer = "zenoh-router"
```

`--why` adds where each fact came from. The emulator, the console and the
serial port are the board descriptor's. The runner passes QEMU
`-nic user,model=lan9118`, which wires the guest's LAN9118 to the user-mode
network; a QEMU line of your own that drops it (`-nic none`, `-nodefaults`)
leaves the guest with no network.

## Drive cargo yourself

The first build cross-compiles nano-ros's dependencies for
`thumbv7m-none-eabi`, about five minutes; later builds take seconds. To use
cargo directly from an IDE, a CI step or with `--release`, print the exact
cargo line `nros build` runs against the generated entry:

```bash probe=420
nros build --dry-run
```

`nros configure` writes the generated entry and its cargo settings without
building, before you open the workspace in an IDE. Both are regenerated on
every build: never edit them, and never add a `.cargo/config.toml` of your
own to carry board facts. Your own toolchain preferences go where cargo
already looks, a parent directory or `$CARGO_HOME`. See
[When `nros build` drives the build](../../background/how-a-build-becomes-an-image.md#when-nros-build-drives-the-build).

## If it doesn't work

- **No `Publishing:` line over the network:** another router holds the
  `locator`'s port, or a QEMU line of your own dropped the NIC.
- **The talker stalls after you change it:** a callback runs long, and
  nothing preempts it.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshoot](../deploy/troubleshoot.md).
